usage: 현대 attaches directly with no 의; this is the single most common frame 사회 appears in.
Compound noun used constantly in news and essays; note no spacing change, just 사회 + 문제.
working life / getting along in the adult world
Written as one word; means workplace and adult social duties, NOT 'social life' in the party sense.
to go out into society (e.g., after graduating)
에 marks the destination; idiom for entering the workforce and adult world.
examples: 우리 사회에는 문제가 많아요.
There are many problems in our society.
Simple frame: 사회 takes 에 + 는 for 'in (our) society', the location-of-existence particle.
대학을 졸업하면 본격적으로 사회생활을 시작해요.
Once you graduate from university, you really start your working life.
Here 사회생활 = professional/adult life — the everyday meaning a learner must internalize.
인터넷이 우리 사회를 크게 바꿔 놓았어요.
The internet has greatly changed our society.
바꿔 놓다 = 'changed it (and it stays that way)'; the lingering-result auxiliary, natural with 사회.
nuance: 사회 (社會, 社 'community/shrine-group' + 會 'gathering') means 'society' as the whole body of people living together, and as a noun-modifier it stacks directly: 현대 사회, 사회 문제, 사회 복지. The trap for English speakers is 사회생활: it does NOT mean 'social life / hanging out', but working life and managing adult/workplace relationships, so 사회생활을 잘하다 praises someone for handling colleagues and obligations well. Contrast 사회 with 모임 — a 모임 is one concrete small gathering (study group, dinner club), while 사회 is the abstract collective; never use 사회 for 'a get-together'. The particle to learn is 에 for location-of-existence (사회에 문제가 있다), not 에서, when you simply say something exists in society.

Using 사회 for a small social gathering ('let's have a 사회 this weekend'). 사회 is the abstract collective; for a get-together use 모임 (모임이 있어요).

usage: 전통 modifies the next noun attributively with no 의: 전통 문화, 전통 음식, 전통 시장.
지키다 ('protect, keep') is the default verb; you guard a tradition the way you guard a promise.
Adjective form: 전통적인 + noun (전통적인 결혼식 = a traditional wedding).
오랜 ('longtime') is the fixed modifier for time-depth here, never 긴 ('long' in length).
examples: 이 음식은 우리 전통 음식이에요.
This food is our traditional food.
Simplest use: 전통 sits straight in front of 음식 with no particle between them.
이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
이어 가다 = 'carry on / continue (and keep going)'; the habitual collocation with 전통.
저는 전통적인 음악보다 현대 음악을 더 좋아해요.
I like modern music more than traditional music.
Real preference talk: 전통적인 (adjective) modifies 음악, paired against 현대 in a A보다 B 더 frame.
nuance: 전통 (傳統, 傳 'hand down/pass on' + 統 'lineage/unbroken line') is a custom, value, or practice passed down across generations, and the hanja literally pictures an unbroken line being handed on — which is why it carries a respectful, valued tone. Contrast it sharply with 습관 (習慣, 'habit'): 전통 is shared and inherited by a group, while 습관 is one individual's repeated personal routine (제 습관, never 제 전통). For the descriptive 'it is traditional', you must switch to the adjective 전통적이다 → 전통적인 + noun; 전통 alone is the abstract noun. The classic 직역 trap is time-length: English 'a long tradition' tempts 긴 전통, but Korean fixes this as 오랜 전통, because 오랜 expresses depth in time while 긴 means physically long.

usage: 현대 modifies a noun directly: 현대 사회, 현대 미술, 현대 의학 — all without 의.
Adjective form for look-and-feel: 현대적인 디자인 = a modern-style design.
현대 + 인 (person) = the people of the present age; very common in essays and editorials.
in the modern era; coming into modern times
Set sentence-opener equivalent to 'in modern times…'.
examples: 이건 현대 미술이에요.
This is modern art.
Bare frame: 현대 attaches straight to 미술 as a noun-modifier, no particle in between.
현대인은 늘 시간에 쫓기며 살아요.
People today live constantly chased by time.
현대인 = 'modern people'; 시간에 쫓기다 = 'be chased by time', a stock collocation.
이 건물은 전통과 현대가 잘 어우러져 있어요.
This building blends tradition and modernity well.
전통과 현대 is the habitual old-vs-new pairing; 어우러지다 = 'blend in harmony'.
nuance: 현대 (現代, 現 'present/appear' + 代 'age/generation') means the modern or contemporary age and works mainly as a noun-modifier (현대 사회, 현대 미술) rather than standing alone in a sentence. Two contrasts matter. First, time-words: 현대 is a whole era, while 최근/요즘 mean 'recently/these days' — so 'I bought it recently' is 최근에 샀어요, never 현대에 샀어요. Second, register/form: to call a thing 'modern in style' you must use the adjective 현대적이다 → 현대적인 디자인; 현대 디자인 sounds like a fixed genre label, not a description of feel. 현대 is the natural counterweight to 전통 whenever you set up an old-versus-new comparison.

Dropping the adjective form: 'modern-style design' is 현대적인 디자인. Bare 현대 디자인 reads as a genre name, not a description of how something looks.

usage: 국가 is the political-entity word for a country; 나라 is the everyday word for the same idea.
국가 modifies official nouns directly: 국가 정책, 국가 기관, 국가 대표.
Formal tone; heard about public service, soldiers, sacrifice.
국가적 + noun (국가적 행사 = a national-scale event); the 차원 phrase 국가적인 차원에서 is common.
examples: 한국은 민주 국가예요.
Korea is a democratic nation.
Simple definition frame; 국가 functions as the predicate noun with 예요.
이번 행사는 국가적인 차원에서 준비되고 있어요.
This event is being prepared on a national level.
국가적인 차원에서 = 'at a national level', a formal set collocation worth memorizing.
여러 국가가 이 문제를 함께 논의했어요.
Several nations discussed this issue together.
여러 국가 = 'several nations'; 논의하다 = 'discuss (formally)', matching the institutional register.
nuance: 국가 (國家, 國 'country' + 家 'house/family' — literally the 'country-household', the state seen as one great family/estate) is the formal, institutional word for a country as a political and legal entity, at home in news, law, and academic writing. The sharp boundary every learner needs is 국가 vs 나라: they share the same dictionary gloss 'country', but 나라 is the warm everyday word and 국가 is the official one — so 우리 나라 is the natural 'our country', while 우리 국가 sounds stiff and almost wrong in conversation. Choose 국가 only when the focus is the state as an institution (government, policy, sovereignty); pair it with formal modifiers like 민주, 국가적, and the phrase 국가적인 차원에서. Do not confuse 국가 'state/nation' with the identically-pronounced 국가 (國歌) 'national anthem'.

usage: Extremely common in news; 정부 modifies the noun directly with no 의.
발표하다 is the standard verb for official statements by the 정부.
The standard administrative split between national and regional authority.
Heard constantly about funding, benefits, and aid (정부 지원을 받다 = receive government support).
examples: 정부가 새 정책을 발표했어요.
The government announced a new policy.
Core news frame: 정부 + 발표하다, the textbook subject-verb pairing.
많은 사람들이 정부의 결정에 반대하고 있어요.
Many people are opposing the government's decision.
정부의 결정 uses 의 to link two nouns; 반대하다 takes 에 (결정에 반대하다).
정부에서 소상공인을 위한 지원을 늘리기로 했어요.
The government decided to increase support for small business owners.
정부에서: organizations as subjects often take 에서, which sounds slightly more institutional than 가.
nuance: 정부 (政府, 政 'governing/administration' + 府 'office/seat of authority' — literally the 'office of governance') is the government as the concrete administrative body that runs the state. The contrast to lock in is 정부 vs 정치: 정부 is the institution/body, while 정치 (politics) is the activity and field — '정부가 발표했어요' (the body announced) but '정치에 관심 없어요' (not interested in the field). A grammar point unique to organizational subjects: Korean lets you mark 정부 as the actor with 에서 as well as 가 — both 정부에서 발표했어요 and 정부가 발표했어요 are correct, with 에서 feeling a touch more formal/institutional. Pair 정부 with official verbs: 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다, 추진하다.

mistakes: Confusing 정부 with 정치. 정부 is the governing body (정부가 결정하다); 정치 is the field/activity (정치를 하다, 정치에 관심이 있다).
Assuming organizational subjects only take 가. With bodies like 정부, the 에서 form is equally natural: 정부에서 발표했어요 ≈ 정부가 발표했어요.

usage: 관심이 있다/없다 takes 에 on the topic: 정치에 관심이 있다 — never 정치를 관심.
정치 + 인 (person) = a person in politics; 정치가 is a near-equivalent.
Adjective form: 정치적인 문제 = a political issue (often with a sensitive/calculated undertone).
to go into / be active in politics
하다 here means working in the political arena, e.g. running for office.
examples: 저는 정치에 관심이 없어요.
I'm not interested in politics.
Bedrock pattern: interest in a topic is X에 관심이 있다/없다, so 정치 takes 에 here.
요즘 정치 뉴스를 보면 답답할 때가 많아요.
These days, watching political news often feels frustrating.
정치 뉴스 = 'political news'; 답답하다 = 'stifling/frustrating', a very Korean emotion word.
그 문제는 너무 정치적이라서 이야기하기 조심스러워요.
That issue is too political, so I'm careful about discussing it.
정치적이라서 = adjective + 라서 ('because it is…'); shows the cautious tone Koreans attach to 정치.
nuance: 정치 (政治, 政 'governing' + 治 'rule/manage' — literally 'governing and ordering [a state]') is the abstract field and activity of politics. Hold three related words apart: 정치 is the field, 정부 (government) is the concrete body, and 정치인 is an individual politician — so 'a politician' is 정치인/정치가, never the literal 정치 사람. The adjective 정치적이다 labels something 'political', usually with an undertone of being calculated, partisan, or socially sensitive. The particle pitfall is interest: 'interested in politics' is 정치에 관심이 있다 (topic marked with 에), not 정치를 관심이 있다. Culturally, 정치 is treated as a touchy subject, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many Koreans deliberately avoid in polite company.

Saying 정치 사람 for 'politician'. The correct word is 정치인 (or 정치가); 정치 사람 is not idiomatic Korean.

usage: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump, not 나쁘다.
Standard compound (성장 = growth); 경제 성장률 = the economic growth rate.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden).
경제 takes scope modifiers directly: 세계 경제, 한국 경제, 지역 경제.
examples: 요즘 경제가 어려워요.
The economy is tough these days.
Plain version of the key idiom: 경제가 어렵다 = 'the economy is struggling', using 어렵다 not 나쁘다.
정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward (a plan/policy)'.
대중교통을 이용하는 게 훨씬 경제적이에요.
Using public transportation is much more economical.
Here 경제적이다 = 'economical / cost-saving' — the everyday wallet-friendly sense, not 'economic'.
nuance: 경제 (經濟, 經 'manage/govern' + 濟 'aid/relieve' — from 經世濟民 'govern the world and relieve the people') means 'the economy' as a system. The biggest learner trap is the adjective 경제적이다, which splits into TWO everyday meanings: (1) 'economical', i.e. money-saving (버스가 더 경제적이에요), and (2) 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden) — context decides which. Equally important is the slump idiom: to say the economy is doing badly, Korean uses 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다, NOT a literal 경제가 나쁘다, because 어렵다 ('hard, strained') is the conventional collocation. Keep 경제 (the system/field) distinct from 경영 (經營, business management of a company); they look similar but 경영 is running a firm.

usage: 제도 = an organized social system of rules; pairs with 교육, 의료, 복지, 연금.
바꾸다 ('change') and 고치다 ('fix/reform') are the common verbs with 제도.
제도적인 문제 = a systemic problem (the structure's fault, not one person's).
도입하다 ('introduce, adopt') is the formal verb for bringing a 제도 in.
examples: 한국은 의료 제도가 좋아요.
Korea has a good healthcare system.
Simple frame: 의료 제도 sits as the subject; 제도 names the whole system, not a single rule.
회사가 재택근무 제도를 새로 도입했어요.
The company newly introduced a work-from-home system.
제도 + 도입하다, the textbook collocation for adopting a formal system.
이건 한 사람의 잘못이 아니라 제도적인 문제예요.
This isn't one person's fault but a systemic problem.
제도적인 문제 = 'systemic/structural problem'; the adjective shifts blame from a person to the structure.
nuance: 제도 (制度, 制 'regulate/establish' + 度 'measure/standard' — an 'established standard', i.e. a set framework) is an organized system of rules or an institution in the abstract: an education system, welfare system, or company-wide policy framework. Draw two lines. Against 규칙 ('rules'): 제도 is large-scale and structural (교육 제도, the whole system), while 규칙 is the concrete everyday rules you follow (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙). Against 기관 (機關, an organization/agency as a body or building): 제도 is the intangible framework, whereas 기관 is the actual institution you can walk into (정부 기관, 교육 기관). The adjective 제도적이다 is the handy tool for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than one individual's fault.

structuredNuance.t: 제도 is an organized system of rules or an institution in the abstract: an education system, welfare system, or company-wide policy framework. The adjective 제도적이다 is the handy tool for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than one individual's fault.

Draw two lines. Against 규칙 ('rules'): 제도 is large-scale and structural (교육 제도, the whole system), while 규칙 is the concrete everyday rules you follow (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙). Against 기관 (機關, an organization/agency as a body or building): 제도 is the intangible framework, whereas 기관 is the actual institution you can walk into (정부 기관, 교육 기관).
制度, 制 'regulate/establish' + 度 'measure/standard' — an 'established standard', i.e. a set framework.

mistakes: Confusing 제도 with 규칙. 제도 is a large institutional framework (복지 제도); 규칙 is everyday rules (회사 규칙, 게임 규칙).
Using 제도 for a physical institution or building. For the organization/agency you enter, use 기관 (교육 기관) or the specific place name, not 제도.

usage: 지키다 ('keep, observe') is the standard verb; the opposite is 법을 어기다 ('break the law').
법률 modifies formal nouns: 법률 상담, 법률 문제, 법률 전문가.
법률적인 책임 = legal responsibility (as opposed to moral responsibility).
제정하다 ('legislate, enact') is the formal verb; heavy news/legal register.
examples: 새 법률이 다음 달부터 시행돼요.
A new law goes into effect starting next month.
법률 + 시행되다 ('take effect/be enforced'), the formal collocation for laws coming into force.
이 문제는 법률 전문가의 도움이 필요해요.
This issue needs help from a legal expert.
법률 전문가 = 'legal expert'; the 의 links 전문가 to the help that is needed.
모든 국민은 법률 앞에서 평등해요.
All citizens are equal before the law.
법률 앞에서 평등하다 = 'equal before the law', a formal set expression you will see in civics texts.
nuance: 법률 (法律, 法 'law/method' + 律 'statute/rule' — two 'law' characters doubled for the formal sense, i.e. enacted statutes) is the written, official term for 'law' as legislation and the legal system, at home in documents, news, and academic prose. The crucial register split is 법률 vs 법: in everyday speech Koreans shorten it to 법 (법을 어기다 = break the law, 법대로 하다 = do it by the book), so 법률을 어기다 sounds stiff in casual chat — reserve 법률 for official contexts or for laws as a body of legislation. Keep it apart from 법원 (法院, the court — the institution that applies the law) and 변호사 (a lawyer): 법률 is the rules themselves, not the people or place that handle them.

Confusing 법률 with 법원. 법률 is the law itself (the statute); 법원 is the court, the institution that applies and interprets it.

usage: 잡다 ('grab') is the idiomatic verb for gaining political power, not 받다 or 하다.
남용하다 ('misuse, abuse') is a frequent, important pairing in news and politics.
권력 + 자 (person) = someone who holds authority; often carries a critical tone.
다툼 ('fight, struggle') captures open conflict over authority within a group.
examples: 그 사람은 권력이 있어요.
That person has power (authority).
Simplest frame: 권력이 있다 = 'has power' in the authority sense; existence marked with 이.
그 정치인은 권력을 남용해서 결국 자리에서 물러났어요.
That politician abused his power and eventually stepped down.
권력을 남용하다 + 자리에서 물러나다 ('step down from one's post'), natural news-style phrasing.
역사를 보면 권력은 영원하지 않아요.
Looking at history, power is not eternal.
권력은 영원하지 않다 = 'power is not eternal', a reflective set sentence with topic-marking 은.
nuance: 권력 (權力, 權 'authority/right' + 力 'force/might' — 'the force of authority') means political power: the authority to control people, decisions, and resources, and it carries a weighty, frequently negative tone (권력 남용 = abuse of power, 권력 다툼 = power struggle). The boundary learners must respect is 권력 vs 힘 (also 'power'): 힘 is general strength — physical (힘이 세다), emotional (힘을 내다 'cheer up'), or everyday influence — whereas 권력 is reserved for institutional/political authority. So 'he is strong' is 힘이 세요, never 권력이 세요. The verb pitfall is collocation: power is something you 잡다 (seize), 가지다 (have), or 행사하다 (exercise) — there is no 권력을 하다.

english: the people; citizens of a nation
usage: 국민 pairs with 권리 ('rights') and 의무 ('duties') in civic contexts.
전 ('whole') + 국민 = everyone in the country (전 국민이 = all citizens [as subject]).
Fixed compound written as one word; a direct vote by all citizens.
뽑다 ('choose, pick, elect') is the natural verb in election contexts.
examples: 국민이 대통령을 뽑아요.
The people elect the president.
Simple civic frame: 국민이 (subject) + 뽑다; 뽑다 is the everyday verb for 'elect/choose'.
이 정책은 전 국민에게 영향을 줘요.
This policy affects all citizens.
전 국민에게 uses 에게 for the people affected; 영향을 주다 = 'have an effect on'.
국가는 국민의 안전과 행복을 위해 일해야 해요.
The state should work for the safety and happiness of its citizens.
국가 + 국민, the classic civic pairing; 의 links 국민 to 안전과 행복.
nuance: 국민 (國民, 國 'nation' + 民 'people' — 'the people of the nation') means the people as citizens of a particular country: a civic, collective term bound up with rights (권리), duties (의무), and the state. Distinguish it from two neighbors. Against 사람들 ('people' in general): 국민 is people specifically as a national citizenry, so '거리에 사람들이 많아요' (lots of people on the street) could never be 국민. Against 시민 (市民, 'citizens'): 시민 leans toward city residents or civil society (시민 단체 = civic groups, 서울 시민 = Seoul residents), while 국민 frames people in relation to the nation and government. Use 국민 whenever the context is national identity, elections, law, or the state's relationship to its population.
